stances.claim: Over the years, CJP has come to realize that the great truths of Scripture are not cloistered in the pages of the Bible or the walls of the Church -- they are lived in our daily struggles. Easter reminds us that we, too, must pass through our own passion and death to resurrect and enjoy a renewed life. CJP capitalizes-with-quotation-marks the lessons from his 1997 book 'Justice & Faith' and updates them with his own journey (and that of others) through passion, death, and resurrection.

LESSON 1 -- 'Sometimes, Adversities and Misfortunes in Life are Preludes to Greater Victories.' Because CJP's father could not afford the then 15-centavo bus fare from Sampaloc, Manila, CJP was unable to enroll in his school of choice -- UP Diliman, where he had a scholarship. CJP envied classmates who made it there. Yet God had a different path for his passion -- at FEU, CJP was blessed to meet and be taught by Dr. Jovito R. Salonga, a brilliant lawyer just appointed law dean, who became CJP's mentor pushing him beyond his limits when CJP wanted to give up on the bar exam after being hospitalized on the first day. There was also a time CJP felt embittered he could not enjoy his Yale masteral scholarship due to inability to pay airfare -- wallowed in self-pity, but in the end found greater triumph in seeing all his five children travel to and finish their graduate degrees in their chosen US universities. Perhaps providential that CJP later organized his own company that assured them of travel.
stances.rhetorical_move: Lesson-1 anchor + 15-centavo-bus-fare + Salonga-mentor + Yale-airfare-forfeiture + five-children-vindication anecdote sequence

stances.claim: In CJP's journey from a poor newspaper boy to Chief Justice, he saw how adversity forged character -- 'Court battles lost and won, personal bereavements, the weight of public office: each trial sharpened my sense of purpose and deepened my reliance on prayer.' CJP has seen the same in countless Filipinos who, after calamity, rise to rebuild with quiet heroism.

LESSON 2 -- 'Whatever Happens, Do Not Lose Heart.' During the 1982 Hong Kong stock market crash, CJP lost everything he had earned abroad -- heartbroken enough to cause him a heart attack; in fact, many were reported to have committed suicide. Forlorn and poor again, CJP decided to go back to the Philippines and concentrate on law practice. In 1983, CJP joined the Rotary Club of Manila, where he met future President Fidel V. Ramos, who later appointed him to the SC in 1995. Working from that high office was never a walk in the park. After his term, CJP chose to continue creating new meanings in the lives of others through the Foundation for Liberty and Prosperity.

History too bears witness -- Abraham Lincoln lost businesses, suffered devastating electoral defeats, mourned the death of his beloved, and endured a complete nervous breakdown. But through perseverance and unshakable resolve, he rose. At 60, he became President of the United States. Though tragically assassinated, he is hailed as one of the greatest leaders in history. Some of us lose heart after only a few disappointments. But remember -- no matter what happens, keep working and believing. Trust in your capacity to rise above defeat and in God's unfailing power and providence.

LESSON 3 -- 'Have Faith in God.' During CJP's own season of passion and death, he moved among the high and the lowly, the powerful and the weak, the glitterati and the downtrodden -- outwardly active, yet inwardly hollow. CJP's restless pursuits brought no peace, no fulfillment, no sense of purpose. CJP's turning point came in 1986, when he found Jesus Christ and was baptized in the Holy Spirit. That encounter changed everything. CJP understood his own resurrection would be incomplete if he kept God's goodness to himself. Since that day -- though feeling inadequate and unworthy as he often does -- CJP has taken up the mission of bringing His Word to every person he meets, quietly and humbly, never noisily and boisterously.

We know the story well -- Jesus was betrayed, scourged, crowned with thorns, nailed to the cross, and left to die in agony. The suffering was visceral, public, and seemingly final. Hope appeared extinguished. Yet on the third day came the resurrection. This divine pattern mirrors life itself -- a pregnant woman endures months of discomfort and exhaustion; labor brings intense pain; yet she embraces it willingly, out of love; and the reward feels eternal at the sound of the first cry. Without pain and love, there is no new life. In the same way, personal trials -- illness, loss, failure -- often become the soil from which our deeper purpose, stronger relationships, and renewed faith spring forth.

Today, we pray for peace in a world shaken by 'a war none of us wanted, yet one that affects us all.' Though our struggles differ, we collectively bear the weight of these global tensions. The message of Easter is not despair but defiant hope. May we emerge from our suffering not merely as survivors but as victors transformed by our suffering -- more loving, more resilient, more anchored in the God who conquered death itself. That is the ultimate meaning of His passion, death, and resurrection. And that, my friends, is the eternal lesson our bleeding world desperately needs today.

notable_anecdotes: The 15-centavo bus fare from Sampaloc, Manila -- CJP's father could not afford this fare, costing CJP his UP Diliman scholarship -- among the most concrete and humble specific-amount autobiographical anchor in CJP's poverty-narrative corpus (the precise denomination 15-centavo registers the family's economic distance from middle-class travel access).

The FEU-Salonga-mentorship origin story -- Dr. Jovito R. Salonga (later Senate President + Manila Mayor) becoming CJP's law-dean mentor specifically because of the bus-fare misfortune -- captures providence-through-poverty narrative pattern.
The bar-exam first-day hospitalization -- Salonga's intervention as the encouragement that prevented CJP from giving up -- a specific mentor-rescue moment in CJP's professional-formation arc.

The Yale masteral-scholarship forfeiture for inability to afford airfare -- among the most specific second-major economic-handicap CJP discloses + the wallow-in-self-pity admission unusual in CJP's typical-public-stance corpus.
The five-children-all-US-graduate-degrees triumphant inversion of the Yale-forfeiture loss -- completing the providence-through-deferred-victory pattern across one generation.

The 1982 Hong Kong stock market crash + heart attack + many-committed-suicide context -- CJP disclosing personal medical and financial crisis tied to a specific historical economic-event, an unusually intimate disclosure for CJP.
The 1983 Rotary Club of Manila meeting future-FVR -- CJP captures the providence-via-civic-club detail showing the social network that produced his eventual SC appointment.

The Abraham Lincoln biographical-resilience analogue (businesses + electoral defeats + beloved-death + nervous breakdown + President at 60 + assassinated + greatest-leaders status) -- among CJP's most concentrated US-historical-resilience case-studies.

The 1986 'found Jesus Christ and was baptized in the Holy Spirit' framing -- CJP's most precise religious-conversion-date disclosure (Catholic Charismatic Renewal context implied) in his column corpus.
The 'outwardly active, yet inwardly hollow' framing of CJP's pre-1986 spiritual condition -- among CJP's most vulnerable self-characterizations.
The 'quietly and humbly, never noisily and boisterously' framing of CJP's evangelism approach -- a deliberate distancing from prosperity-gospel-televangelism style.
The pregnant-woman-and-first-cry analogue for resurrection-pattern -- CJP's distinctive biological-natalist illustration of pain-love-new-life pattern.

The 'war none of us wanted, yet one that affects us all' framing -- likely referring to Iran-US-Israel and/or Russia-Ukraine (the column appears between A28 Iran column April 13 and earlier-March columns), captured as collective-burden framing.
The 'bleeding world' closing-epithet -- a striking visceral-image closing CJP's Easter column with global-distress framing.
